It is an act jure imperii: a minister's use of lethal force abroad is an exercise of sovereign power, not commercial or private-law activity, and *Germany v. Italy* (ICJ 2012) holds that unlawfulness doesn't change that characterization. The team note is wrong. Ministers' acts are not always personal conduct, and foreign courts cannot hear any case against a minister regardless of the act's nature. A serving minister has personal immunity (ratione personae), and after leaving office they keep functional immunity (ratione materiae) for official acts. Immunity can still be denied through the territorial tort exception if the killing happened in the forum state (e.g. UN Convention Art. 12), or for international crimes in the case of a former official.
